---
title: "`arsgrammatica`'s graph of syntactic relations"
---


::: {.callout-note}
In `arsgrammatica` the `TokenAnalysis` class is the primary implementation of these ideas.
:::


When `arsgrammatica` analyses a passage of Latin, every non-punctuation token is related in a graph structure to one or more of the following: other tokens in the text, implied tokens, or a hypothetical root element. This page summarizes all relationship categories that `arsgrammatica` recognizes. For ease of human reading, examples are presented in a simple tabular form not identical to the [format used to serialize analyses](../reference/analysisformat.qmd).


## Constructions of verbal expressions

### Independent clause

Verbs of independent (main) clauses are  related to a hypothetical `root` value as `unit verb`. 


**Example**: *arma virumque cano*.

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *cano*  | `unit verb` | (`root`) |





#### Compound verb forms

All compound forms using *sum* with a participle treat the participle as the verb of the verbal unit and the form of *sum* as an auxiliary. The participle therefore is related to its context just as any other verbal expression would be. The form of *sum* relates to the participle as `auxiliary`.

**Example**: *urbs condita est*.


| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *condita* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| *est* | `auxiliary` | *condita* |

Similarly, when gerundive forms are in predicate position with a form of *sum*, the gerundive + *sum* is treated as a compound form. The gerundive is classified like any other finite or infinitive form, and the form of *sum* relates to it as `auxiliary`.

**Example**: *Carthago delenda est*.

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *delenda* | `unit verb` | (`root`) | 
| *est* | `auxiliary` | *delenda* |


### Directly quoted speech

Finite verbs in directly quoted speech are related to the verb introducing the quotation as `direct quote`.

**Example**: *'hanc ego aram' inquit 'Pudicitiae plebeiae dedico'*.

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *dedico* | `direct quote` | *inquit* |
| *inquit* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |


Further constructions governed by the direct speech, such as subordinate clauses, are treated the same way they would be treated after an independent clause

**Example**: "Vos,” inquit, “videritis quid balteo conveniat."


| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Vos* | `subject` | *videritis* |
| *inquit* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| *videritis* | `direct quote` | *inquit* |
| *quid* | `subordinating word` | *videritis* | 
| *balteo* | `dative` | *conveniat* | 
| *conveniat* | `unit verb` | *quid* |


### Aside

When the syntax of the sentence is interrupted by an independent verbal expression, the verb of the interrupting expression is related to the verb of the interrupted context as `aside`.

**Example**:  *Sp. Nautius -- Octavium Maecium quidam eum tradunt -- cum auxiliaribus cohortibus erat*.

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
|*tradunt* | `aside` | *erat* |
| *erat* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |



### Dependent clause

When a dependent clause is introduced by a subordinating word or by a relative pronoun, the verb relates to the subordinating word or reative pronoun as `unit verb`. 


**Example**: *Hercules cum gregem perlustrasset, pergit ad proximam speluncam.*

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *perlustrasset* | `unit verb` | *cum* |
| *pergit* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |

### Parataxis

Several verbs expressing ideas connected with necessity, wishes, preferences or commands (such as *oportet*, *necesse est*, *volo*, *peto*, or imperative *fac*) can be constructed with a clause in the subjunctive without any subordinating word. 

In this construction, the subordinate verbal unit is related to the governing verb with the relationship `parataxis`.

**Example**: *Precor eam videam.*

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Precor* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| *videam* | `parataxis` | *Precor* |

**Example**: *Tu velim ad me scribas.*


| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *velim* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| *scribas* | `parataxis` | *velim* |


### Indirect statement

Infinitive forms in indirect statement relate to the verb of speaking as `indirect statement`.

**Example**: *id philtrum esse dixit*.

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *esse* | `indirect statement` | *dixit* |
| *dixit* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |

### Circumstantial participle

Circumstantial participles express a verbal idea that is related to an antecedent substantive in the relation `circumstantial participle`.

**Example**: *adveniens vir Tarquiniique excepti benigne.*

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *adveniens* | `circumstantial participle` | *vir* |
| *excepti* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| (`implied sum`)  | `auxiliary` | *excepti* |


### Gerundive

As noted in documentation of [verbal units](./verbalunits.qmd), when a gerundive form is in attributive position with a substantive, it has `gerundive` as its type of verbal unit. In this construction, the gerundive relates to its governing substantive with relationship `gerundive`.

**Example**: *Legatos ad eum mittunt ad pacem faciendam.*

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *mittunt* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| *ad* | `adverbial` | *mittunt* |
| *pacem* | `object of preposition` | *ad* |
| *faciendam* | `gerundive` | *pacem* |

(See below on constructions of prepositional phrases.)


Reminder: when gerundives are part of a compound form with *sum*, they are *not* linked to a substantive in the syntax graph, but instead are treated like any other finite or infinitive verb form.

**Counter example**: *tantam dimicationem subeundam non sine periculo esse intellegebat*

Here, *subeundam esse* is a compound form in indirect statement after *intellegebat*, with accusative subject *dimicationem*.



| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *subeundam* | `indirect statement` | *intellegebat* | 
| *esse* | `auxiliary` | *subeundam* |
| *intellegebat* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |




## Other constructions with verbs


### Complementary infinitive

When an infinitive is used to complete the semantics of a verbal expression with certain verbs such as *volo*, the infinitive relates to the verbal expression as `complementary infinitive`.


**Example**: *ascribi se in eam civitatem voluit*.

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *ascribi* | `complementary infinitive` | *voluit* |
| *voluit* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |






## A-A-T relations

The Agent-Action-Target model focuses on two special relations to verbal expressions: the agent and the target. In Latin (as in English), these relations are constructed differently depending on the voice of the verbal expression. 

In active-voice verbs and deponent verbs, agency is expressed by the `subject` relationship. If the verb has a `direct object`, the object is the target of the A-A-T model. If a linking verb (copula) has a substantive `predicate`, the predicate is the target. Note that non-nominative predicates (illustrated below) are not treated as targets in the A-A-T model.

In passive voice verbs that are not deponent, the `subject` relationship expresses the target. This is also true for gerundive constructed with *sum* (passive periphrastic). Agency is expressed either by the `agent-ablative` or the `agent-dative` relationship.

### Subject

A substantive functioning as the grammatical subject of a verbal expression is related to it as `subject`.


**Example**: *Lucumo Demarati Corinthii filius erat*.

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Lucumo* | `subject` | *erat* |
| *erat* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| *filius* | `predicate` | *erat* |


### Agent


The headword of a prepositional phrase expressing agency with passive verbs (that is, `a`/`ab`) relates to the verbal expression as `agent-ablative`.

**Example**: *urbs a Romulo condita est*.


| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *urbs* | `subject` | *condita* |
| *a* | `agent-ablative` | *condita* |
| *Romulo* | `object of preposition` | *a* |
| *condita* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| *est* | `auxiliary` | *condita* |

> See below on objects of prepositions.


When the gerundive is in a compound construction with an explicit or implicit form of *sum*, agency is expressed by a substantive in the dative case, which is related as `agent-dative`.

**Example**: *Caesari omnia uno tempore erant agenda*

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Caesari* | `agent-dative` | *agenda* |
| *erant* | `auxiliary` | *agenda* |
| *agenda* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |

Compound forms of the perfect sometimes admit a similar construction.


**Example**: *res silentio praeterita nobis est.*

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *res* | `subject` | *praeterita* | 
| *praeterita* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| *nobis* | `agent-dative` | *praeterita* | 
| *est* | `auxiliary` | *praeterita* |


Note that datives with an attributive `gerundive` are in a simple `dative` relation to the gerundive. Datives with a passive verbs are not common, and do not occur with simple (non-compound) forms.

### Direct object


The direct object of a transitive active verb is related to the verbal expression as `direct object`.

**Example**: *Tarquinium mala libido Lucretiae per vim stuprandae capit*.



| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Tarquinium* | `direct object` | *capit* |
| *libido* | `subject` | *capit* |
| *capit* | `unit verb` | (`root`)|




### Predicate

We use the `predicate` relation in four ways. 

1) Substantives or adjectives serving as predicates of linking (copulative) verbs. These are *targets* in the A-A-T model.

**Example**: *Lucumo Demarati Corinthii filius erat*.


| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Lucumo* | `subject` | *erat* |
| *filius* | `predicate` | *erat* |
| *erat* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |

2) A substantive describing the role or state in which the subject performs an action. Note that these are *not* targets in the A-A-T model.

**Example**: *Lucumo superfuit patri bonorum omnium heres.*

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Lucumo* | `subject` | *superfuit* | 
| *superfuit* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| *heres* | `predicate` | *superfuit* |


3) A substantive describing the direct object of a verb qualifying the result of the action, typically after verbs of naming, calling, thinking, judging or showing such as  *appellare, vocare, creare, facere, habere, iudicare, putare, aestimare, se praebere*, or  *reddere*. We relate these as `predicate` to the substantive direct object. Note that these are *not* targets in the A-A-T model.

**Example**: *Ciceronem consulem creaverunt.*


| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Ciceronem* | `direct object` | *creaverunt* | 
| *consulem* | `predicate` | *Ciceronem*|
| *creaverunt* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |

4) A substantive predicate in the passive-voice equivalent of category three is in a `predicate` relation to the passive verb, and constitutes an AAT target.

**Example**: *Cicero consul creatus est.*

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Cicero* | `subject` | *creatus* |
| *consul* | `predicate` | *creatus* |
| *creatus*  | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| *est* | `auxiliary` | *creatus* |


## Case constructions with substantives

Apart from the special A-A-T relations, `arsgrammatica` does not subdivide syntactic constructions of substantives by their semantics. Instead, it identifies the case that constitutes the syntactic relationship. `arsgrammatica` leaves it to subsequent semantic analysis to decide if, for example, a `genitive` relation between two nouns expresses possession, a partitive idea, material or units of measure, or whether the relationship is a subjective or objective action. 

### Genitive


When a substantive in the genitive case modifies another substantive, the relationship is `genitive`.

**Example**: *hic filius erat regis*.



| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *hic* | `subject` | *erat* | 
| *filius* | `predicate` | *erat* |
| *erat* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| *regis* | `genitive` | *filius* |



### Dative

When a substantive in the dative case is related to a verb or another substantive, the relationship is `dative`.


**Example of relationship to verb**: *documentum mortalibus dedero*.

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *mortalibus* | `dative` | *dedero* |
| *dedero* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |

**Example of relationship to a substantive**: *te mihi mater aucturum caelestium numerum cecinit*


| Token | relationship | related token | 
| --- | --- | --- |
| *mihi* | `dative` |  *mater* | 
| *mater* | `subject` | *cecinit* |
| *cecinit* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |



### Accusative

When an accusative noun is related to a noun, or when it relates to a verb but does *not* express a direct object relationship, the relationship value is `accusative`.

**Example**: *Romam venit*.

The verb *venit* is intransitive, but *Romam* relates to it.


| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Romam* | `accusative` | *venit* |
| *venit* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |

**Example**: *duo milia passuum iter fecerunt*.

The phrase *duo milia passuum* qualifies the noun *iter* with a length of distance specified in the accusative. 


| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *milia* | `accusative` | *iter* | 
| *passuum* | `genitive` | *milia* |
| *iter* | `direct object` | *fecerunt* | 
| *fecerunt* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |


### Ablative

When nouns in the ablative case are related to another noun or to a verb, the relationship is `ablative`.

**Example**: *omnia ferro flammaque miscet*


| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *ferro* | `ablative` | *miscet* |
| *flamma* | `ablative` | *miscet* |
| *miscet* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |


**Example**: *Collatinus negat verbis opus esse*.


| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Collatinus* | `subject` | *negat* | 
| *negat* | `unit verb` | (`root`) | 
| *verbis* | `ablative` | *opus* |
| *opus* | `subject` | *esse* |
| *esse* | `indirect statement` | *negat* |


### Vocative 

Nouns in the vocative case are related to a verbal expression as `vocative`.


**Example**: *Non est ita, domine*.



| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *est* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| *domine* | `vocative` | *est* |





## Substantives from verbal roots

In addition to the previously discussed constructions, the infinitive may be used as a nominative singular noun naming the action of a verbal idea (e.g., *amare* = "the act of loving"). In the oblique cases, the gerund is used to name the action of a verbal idea. The syntactic relationships of these substantive forms are treated exactly the same way as any other substantives.

**Example**: *dolere malum est.*

The infinitive *dolere* is the subject of the verb *est*. 

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *dolere* | `subject` | *est* |
| *malum* | `predicate` | *est* |
| *est* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |

As in all infinitive constructions, the infinitive, like any other verbal form, may have objects; if a subject is explicitly given, it will be in the accusative case.


**Example**: *Ingenuas didicisse fideliter artes emollit mores.*


| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *didicisse* | `subject` | *emollit* |
| *artes* | `direct object` | *didicisse* |
| *emollit* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| *mores* | `direct object` | *emollit* |



**Example**: *Multo labore constat ars dicendi.*

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *labore* | `ablative` | *constat* |
| *constat* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| *ars* | `subject` | *constat* |
| *dicendi* | `genitive` | *ars* |


## Adverbial and adjectival expressions


### Adverbs 

Adverbs and other adverbial expressions (such as prepositional phrases with an adverbial sense)   have the relationship of `adverbial` to the token they qualify, whether the token is verbal, substantive or adjectival.

**Example**: *ad Ianiculum forte ventum erat*.

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *forte* | `adverbial` | *ventum* |
| *ventum* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| *erat* | `auxiliary` | *ventum* |


### Adjectives

If an adjective is used as a substantive, it is treated just like any other substantive. If it describes a substantive, it has the relationship `adjectival` to that substantive. This example illustrates both an adjective used substantively (*bonorum*) and an adjective used adjectivally (*omnium*)

**Example**: *Lucumo superfuit patri bonorum omnium heres*,


| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Lucumo* | `subject` | *superfuit* |
| *superfuit* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| *bonorum* | `genitive` | *heres* |
| *omnium* | `adjectival` | *bonorum* |
| *heres* | `predicate` | `superfuit` |


**Example**: *hiberna aberant ab eo milia passuum XXV.* 

In this example, the numeric adjective *viginti quinque* is written with a numeric token *XXV*.


| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *hiberna* | `subject` | *aberant* |
| *aberant* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| *ab* | `adverbial` | *aberant* |
| *eo* | `object of preposition` | *ab* |
| *milia* | `accusative` | *aberant* |
| *passuum* | `genitive` | *milia* |
| *XXV* | `adjectival` | *milia* |





### Prepositional phrases

Prepositional phrases most frequently function adverbially. In this construction the preposition is related to a verb or adjective with the `adverbial` relationship. Less frequently, a prepositional phrase serves as an adjectival description of a substantive. In these constructions, the preposition relates to the substantive as `adjectival`. Nouns functioning as objects of prepositions, whatever their case, relate to the preposition as `object of preposition`.

**Example of an adverbial phrase**: *ad Ianiculum forte ventum erat.*


| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *ad* | `adverbial` | *ventum* |
| *Ianiculum* | `object of preposition` | *ad* |
| *forte* | `adverbial` | *ventum* |
| *ventum* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| *erat* | `auxiliary` | *ventum* |




**Example of an adjectival phrase**:  *nuntius victoriae ad Cannas Carthaginem venerat*

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *nuntius* | `subject` | *venerat* |
| *victoriae* | `genitive` | *nuntius* | 
| *ad* | `adjectival` | *victoriae* |
| *Cannas* | `object of preposition` | *ad* |
| *Carthaginem* | `accusative` | *venerat* |
| *venerat* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |



## Special substantive relations


### Ablative absolute

Substantives modified by a participle can be used  in the ablative case without other syntactic connection to the governing verbal expression (that is, they are syntactically *absolute*). In this construction, the noun has the relationship `ablative absolute` to the governing verb. The participle is treated as any other circumstantial participle.

**Example**: *Anco regnante Lucumo Romam commigravit*.




| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Anco* | `ablative absolute` | *commigravit* |
| *regnante* | `circumstantial participle` | *Anco* |
| *Lucumo* | `subject` | *commigravit* |
| *Romam* | `accusative` | *commigravit* |
| *commigravit* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |


### Apposition

When a substantive stands in apposition to another substantive, it has the relationship `apposition`; the first substantive is constructed normally.

**Example**: *Neptunus et Aegeus Pandionis filius in fano Mineruae cum Aethra Pitthei filia una nocte concubuerunt.*

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Neptunus* | `subject` | *concubuerunt* |
| *Aegeus* | `subject` | *concubuerunt* |
| *Pandionis* | `genitive` | *filius* |
| *filius* | `apposition` | *Aegeus* |
| *cum* | `adverbial` | *concubuerunt* |
| *Aethra* | `object of preposition` | *cum* |
| *Pitthei* | `genitive` | *filia* |
| *filia* | `apposition` | *Aethra* |
| *una* | `adjectival` | *nocte* | 
| *nocte* | `ablative` | *concubuerunt* | 
| *concubuerunt* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |




### Praenomen


A token that `arsgrammatica` classifies as `praenomen` is often used in conjunction with a fully spelled out *nomen* or *cognomen*. In these constructions, we relate it to the name with relatinship `praenomen`.

**Example**: *Sp. Nautius – Octavium Maecium quidam eum tradunt – cum auxiliaribus cohortibus erat.*


| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Sp.* | `praenomen` | *Nautius* |
| *Nautius* | `subject` | *erat* |
| *erat* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |



When, on the other hand, a `praenomen` appears without a *nomen* or *cognomen*, we treat it as we would any other substantive.

**Example of `praenomen` token as a substantive**:  *M. Agrippa L. f. cos. tertium fecit*

In this sentence, the token *M.* is in relation of `praenomen` with *Agrippa*. The token *L.*, on the other hand, refers to an individual with praenomen only, without corresponding nomen. Here, we take it be a genitive form *L(ucii)* standing in `genitive` relationship to *f.* We take the abbreviations *f.* and *cos.* to be nominatives in apposition to *Agrippa*, *L(ucii) f(ilius)* and *co(n)s(ul)*.

| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *M.* | `praenomen` | *Agrippa* |
| *Agrippa* | `subject` | *fecit* |
| *L.* | `genitive` | *f.* |
| *f.* | `apposition` | *Agrippa* |
| *cos.* | `apposition` | *Agrippa* |
| *tertium* | `adverbial` | *cos.* |
| *fecit* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |


## Coordinating and subordinating words


### Coordinating word

When words like *igitur*, *autem*, *sed*, *ceterum* and *nam* (among many others) join a verbal expression to a preceding sentence, we relate the coordinating word to the verb as a `coordinating word`.

**Example**: *audiens autem Iacob quod alimenta venderentur in Aegypto dixit filiis suis quare neglegitis?*


| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *audiens* | `circumstantial participle` | *Iacob* |
| *autem* | `coordinating word` | *dixit* |
| *Iacob* | `subject` | *dixit* |


When a coordinating word like *et*, *aut* or the post-positive *que* connects a pair of items, we relate the connecting word to both items with `coordinating word` as the value for relationship type. 


**Example**: *suo tempore peperit Chrysen iuniorem et dixit se ab Apolline concepisse.* 

The conjunction *et* joins two independent verbal expressions.

| Token | relationship| related token | 
| --- | --- | --- | 
| *peperit* | `unit verb` | (`root`) | 
| *et* (t5) | `coordinating word` | *peperit* | 
| *et* (t5) | `coordinating word` | *dixit* |
| *dixit* | `unit verb` | (`root`) | 



Note that when joining verbal expressions, the coordinating word may not be close in word order to the verbal token itself.

**Example**: *ille fidem suam infirmare noluit, Hermionenque ab Oreste adduxit*.

The coordinating word *que* joins two verbal expressions.

| Token | relationship | related token | 
| --- | --- | --- | 
| *noluit* | `unit verb` | (`root`) | 
| *Hermionen* | `direct object` | *adduxit* | 
| *que* (t7) | `coordinating word` | *noluit* | 
| *que* (t7) | `coordinating word` | *adduxit* |
| *adduxit* | `unit verb` | (`root`) | 



An important detail to note is that the word *et* can be used as a conjunction or adverbially ("even", "also")! 

**Example**: *Tu quoque, Brute, fili mi, et tu?* 

Here the token *et* is functioning as an adverb, not a conjunction. It will have the lexical token *tu* as its `relation`, with the `relationship` value *adverbial*.


We use exactly the same annotation when coordinating words connect other kinds of items than verbal expressions.




**Example**: *arma virumque cano*.


| Token | relationship| related token | 
| --- | --- | --- |
| *arma* | `direct object` | *cano* | 
| *virum* | `direct object` | *cano* | 
| *que*  (t2) | `coordinating word` | *arma* | 
| *que*  (t2) |`coordinating word` | *virum* |
| *cano* | `unit verb` | (`root`) | 



Note that conjunctions like *et* and *aut* can be repeated to form connecting pairs or even series of conjunctions (e.g. *et..et..et*). If the repetition has the form *A et B et C*, we annotate each conjunction as connecting a pair of elements: the first *et* connects *A* and *B*, the second *et* connects *B* and *C*. If, however, the series has repetitions like *et A et B et C*, we relate the first, introductory conjunction only to the first element *A*; subsequent conjunctions are annotated as usual. 

**Example**: *Spectaculorum et assiduitate et varietate et magnificentia omnes antecessit*.


Three ablative expressions, *assiduitate*,  *varietate*, and *magnificentia*, are each introduced by *et*.  


| Token | relationship | related token | 
| --- | --- | --- | 
| *et* (t1) | `coordinating word` | *assiduitate* | 
| *assiduitate* | `ablative` | *antecessit* | 
| *et* (t3) (second instance)| `coordinating word` | *assiduitate* | 
| *et* (t3) (second instance) |`coordinating word` | *varietate* | 
| *varietate* | `ablative` | *antecessit* | 
| *et* (t5) (third instance) | `coordinating word` | *varietate* |
| *et* (t5) (third instance) | `coordinating word` | *magnificentia* |
| *magnificentia* | `ablative` | *antecessit* |
| *omnes* | `direct object` | *antecessit* | 
| *antecessit* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |



### Subordinating word


When subordinating words like *ut*, *cum*, *ne*, *quoniam*, *quo*, *quod*, and *si* (among many others) or words introducing an indirect question join a verbal expression to a preceding expression, we relate the subordinating word to the verb as a `subordinating word`.



**Example**: *Hercules cum gregem perlustrasset, pergit ad proximam speluncam.*



| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *cum* | `subordinating word` | *pergit* |
| *perlustrasset* | `unit verb` | *cum* |
| *pergit* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |




**Example**: *scias oportet quid discas.*


| Token | relationship | related token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *scias* | `parataxis` | *oportet* |
| *oportet* | `unit verb` | (`root`) | 
| *quid* | `subordinating word` | *scias* | 
| *discas* | `unit verb` | *quid* |

The interrogative pronoun introducing indirect questions needs to be carefully distinguished from the relative pronoun (next section), with which it shares many identical forms.


### Relative pronoun

When a subordinate clause is introduced by a form of the relative pronoun, we must relate the relative to two different tokens: its antecedent in the governing clause, and to a token showing its function in the relative clause.

**Example**: *Latini, cum quibus Tullo regnante ictum foedus erat, sustulerant animos.*

The relative pronoun *quibus* refers to *Latini* in the main clause. In the relative clause, it is the object of the preposition *cum*.



| Token | relationship  | related token |
| --- | --- | --- | 
| *Latini* | `subject` | *sustulerant* | 
| *cum* | `adverbial` | *ictum* | 
| *quibus* (t3) | `relative pronoun` | *Latini* | 
| *quibus* (t3) | `object of preposition` | *cum* |
| *ictum* | `unit verb` | *quibus* |  
| *foedus* | `subject` | *ictum* | 
| *erat* | `auxiliary` | *ictum* |  
| *sustulerant* | `unit verb` | (`root`) | 
| *animos* | `direct object` | *sustulerant* | 



## Syntactic dependencies of implied tokens


The discussion of [tokenization](./tokens.qmd) identified three categories of *implied* tokens that `arsgrammatica` recognizes:  `implied sum`, `implied verb`, `implied substantive`. These implied nodes will appear in the token table with text value `None`. We treat their syntactic relations in exactly the same way as if they were  instantiated by a real token in the text. 

### Implied *sum*

**Example**: *omnia praeclara rara.* 

This is a complete sentence, with a subject phrase *omnia praeclara* and a predicate *rara*, implying a form of *sum* for the unit verb.

| Token | relationship | related token | 
| --- | --- | --- | 
| *omnia* | `adjectival` | *praeclara* |
| *praeclara* | `subject` | (`implied sum`) |
| (`implied sum`) | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| *rara* | `predicate` | (`implied sum`) |


 
**Example**: *inde P. Valerius iterum T. Lucretius consules facti.* 

This sentence has a single verbal expression with a perfect passive verb, *facti* with *sunt* omitted. 

| Token | relationship | related token | 
| --- | --- | --- | 
| *facti* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| (`implied sum`) | `auxiliary` | *facti* |
 


### Implied verb

**Example**:  *nimium Tarquinios regno adsuesse; initium a Prisco factum; regnasse dein Ser. Tullium*. 


Here three verbal expressions are each constructed in indirect statement. They imply a verb of speaking governing all three verbal expressions.

| Token | relationship | related token | 
| --- | --- | --- | 
| *Tarquinios* | `subject` | *adsuesse* |
| *adsuesse* | `indirect statement` | (`implied verb`) |
| (`implied verb`) | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| *initium* | `subject` | *factum* |
| *factum* | `indirect statement` | (`implied verb`) |
| (`implied sum`) | `auxiliary` | *factum* |
| *regnasse* | `indirect statement` | (`implied verb`)
| *Ser.* | `praenomen` | *Tullium* |
| *Tullium* | `subject` | *regnasse* |



### Implied substantive

**Example**: *quem dii amant adolescens moritur.*

Here the relative pronoun *quem* assumes an unexpressed antecedent functioning as the subject of the main clause, "(He) dies young whom the gods love."

| Token | relationship  | related token  | 
| --- | --- | --- | 
| *quem* (t0) | `relative pronoun` | (`implied substantive`) | 
| *quem* (t0) | `direct object` | *amant* |
| *dii* | `subject` | *amant* | 
|*amant* | `unit verb` | *quem* | 
| *adolescens* | `predicate` | *moritur* | 
| *moritur* | `unit verb` | (`root`) | 
| (`implied substantive`) | `subject` | *moritur* | 



**Example**: *quasi ad alienos durius loquebatur, interrogans eos: Unde venistis?*

The participle *interrogans* depends on an unexpressed antecedent referring to the subject of *loquebatur*. 


| Token | relationship | related token  | 
| --- | --- | --- | 
| *loquebatur* | `unit verb` | (`root`) |
| *interrogans* | `circumstantial participle` | (`implied substantive`) |
| *Unde* | `adverbial` | *venistis* |
| *venistis* | `direct quote` | *interrogans* |
| (`implied substantive`) | `subject` | *loquebatur* |
